    OPT   Est. Speedup: 38.01%                                                                                          
          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          60.65% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.

    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 30.56%                                                                                          
          On average, each warp of this workload spends 17.2 cycles being stalled waiting for an immediate constant     
          cache (IMC) miss. A read from constant memory costs one memory read from device memory only on a cache miss;  
          otherwise, it just costs one read from the constant cache. Accesses to different addresses by threads within  
          a warp are serialized, thus the cost scales linearly with the number of unique addresses read by all threads  
          within a warp. As such, the constant cache is best when threads in the same warp access only a few distinct   
          locations. If all threads of a warp access the same location, then constant memory can be as fast as a        
          register access. This stall type represents about 30.6% of the total average of 56.4 cycles between issuing   
          two instructions.                                                                                             
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 0.05729%                                                                                        
          Instructions are executed in warps, which are groups of 32 threads. Optimal instruction throughput is         
          achieved if all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. The chosen launch configuration, early     
          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 7.8 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced   
          to 7.7 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.       
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

          9.08% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each        
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.

          all sectors requested in L2.                                                                                  
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation

    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 30.35%                                                                                          
          On average, each warp of this workload spends 17.3 cycles being stalled waiting for an immediate constant     
          cache (IMC) miss. A read from constant memory costs one memory read from device memory only on a cache miss;  
          otherwise, it just costs one read from the constant cache. Accesses to different addresses by threads within  
          a warp are serialized, thus the cost scales linearly with the number of unique addresses read by all threads  
          within a warp. As such, the constant cache is best when threads in the same warp access only a few distinct   
          locations. If all threads of a warp access the same location, then constant memory can be as fast as a        
          register access. This stall type represents about 30.3% of the total average of 57.0 cycles between issuing   
          two instructions.                                                                                             
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    INF   Check the Warp Stall Sampling (All Samples) table for the top stall locations in your source based on

          on each stall reason.                                                                                         
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 0.05974%                                                                                        
          Instructions are executed in warps, which are groups of 32 threads. Optimal instruction throughput is         
          achieved if all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. The chosen launch configuration, early     
          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 7.8 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced   
          to 7.7 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.       
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 38.13%                                                                                          
          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          61.08% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling                                                
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers),          
          accounting for 0.07% of the local memory load (LDL) and 4.07% of the local store (STL) instructions. 10.43%   
          of all local loads and 93.78% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 89.03% of all       
          sectors requested in L2. The local memory accesses of this workload amount to 11.78% of all executed          
          instructions.                                                                                                 
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).                         
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 52.01%                                                                                          
          The memory access pattern for global loads from L1TEX might not be optimal. On average, only 3.9 of the 32    
          bytes transmitted per sector are utilized by each thread. This could possibly be caused by a stride between   
          threads. Check the Source Counters section for uncoalesced global loads.

          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice

    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 30.08%                                                                                          
          On average, each warp of this workload spends 17.3 cycles being stalled waiting for an immediate constant     
          cache (IMC) miss. A read from constant memory costs one memory read from device memory only on a cache miss;  
          otherwise, it just costs one read from the constant cache. Accesses to different addresses by threads within  
          a warp are serialized, thus the cost scales linearly with the number of unique addresses read by all threads  
          within a warp. As such, the constant cache is best when threads in the same warp access only a few distinct   
          locations. If all threads of a warp access the same location, then constant memory can be as fast as a        
          register access. This stall type represents about 30.1% of the total average of 57.6 cycles between issuing   
          two instructions.                                                                                             
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          on each stall reason.                                                                                         
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 0.05898%                                                                                        
          Instructions are executed in warps, which are groups of 32 threads. Optimal instruction throughput is         
          achieved if all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. The chosen launch configuration, early     
          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 7.8 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced   
          to 7.7 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.       
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

    OPT   Est. Local Speedup: 51.36%                                                                                    
          Every scheduler is capable of issuing one instruction per cycle, but for this workload each scheduler only    
          issues an instruction every 11.2 cycles. This might leave hardware resources underutilized and may lead to    
          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 10.82 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.13 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible      
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per      
          warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections can help, too.

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 3.906%                                                                                          
          Instructions are executed in warps, which are groups of 32 threads. Optimal instruction throughput is         
          achieved if all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. The chosen launch configuration, early     
          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 17.3 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced  
          to 15.7 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.      
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

    OPT   Est. Speedup: 38.12%                                                                                          
          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          61.21% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling                                                
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers),          
          accounting for 0.07% of the local memory load (LDL) and 4.07% of the local store (STL) instructions. 10.33%   
          of all local loads and 93.61% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 88.86% of all       
          sectors requested in L2. The local memory accesses of this workload amount to 11.78% of all executed          
          instructions.                                                                                                 
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).                         
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 30.31%                                                                                          
          On average, each warp of this workload spends 17.4 cycles being stalled waiting for an immediate constant     
          cache (IMC) miss. A read from constant memory costs one memory read from device memory only on a cache miss;  
          otherwise, it just costs one read from the constant cache. Accesses to different addresses by threads within  
          a warp are serialized, thus the cost scales linearly with the number of unique addresses read by all threads  
          within a warp. As such, the constant cache is best when threads in the same warp access only a few distinct   
          locations. If all threads of a warp access the same location, then constant memory can be as fast as a        
          register access. This stall type represents about 30.3% of the total average of 57.4 cycles between issuing   
          two instructions.                                                                                             
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          on each stall reason.                                                                                         
    ----- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    OPT   Est. Speedup: 0.05912%                                                                                        
          Instructions are executed in warps, which are groups of 32 threads. Optimal instruction throughput is         
          achieved if all 32 threads of a warp execute the same instruction. The chosen launch configuration, early     
          thread completion, and divergent flow control can significantly lower the number of active threads in a warp  
          per cycle. This workload achieves an average of 7.8 threads being active per cycle. This is further reduced   
          to 7.7 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.       
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

          to 15.9 threads per warp due to predication. The compiler may use predication to avoid an actual branch.      
          Instead, all instructions are scheduled, but a per-thread condition code or predicate controls which threads  
          execute the instructions. Try to avoid different execution paths within a warp when possible.

          This workload accesses local memory                                                                           
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses), accounting for     
          61.35% of all sectors requested in L1TEX. Local memory refers to a memory space that is private to each       
          thread. Although it is logically distinct, local memory resides in global memory. This can lead to higher     
          memory latency compared to the usage of registers or shared memory, a decrease in available bandwidth to      
          global memory, and an increase in executed instructions.                                                      
          Some of the local memory accesses are due to register spilling                                                
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#variable-memory-space-specifiers),          
          accounting for 0.15% of the local memory load (LDL) and 7.21% of the local store (STL) instructions. 9.19%    
          of all local loads and 96.30% of all local stores spill into the L2 cache, accounting for 86.98% of all       
          sectors requested in L2. The local memory accesses of this workload amount to 11.66% of all executed          
          instructions.                                                                                                 
          One common reason for the use of local memory is arrays being too large to fit into registers or not being    
          indexed using compile time constants (see the "Local Memory" section of the CUDA Programming Guide            
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#device-memory-accesses). For more advice    
          on how to reduce the usage of local memory refer to the documentation                                         
          (https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-hw-memory).

          less optimal performance. Out of the maximum of 12 warps per scheduler, this workload allocates an average    
          of 1.98 active warps per scheduler, but only an average of 0.45 warps were eligible per cycle. Eligible       
          warps are the subset of active warps that are ready to issue their next instruction. Every cycle with no      
          eligible warp results in no instruction being issued and the issue slot remains unused. To increase the       
          number of eligible warps, avoid possible load imbalances due to highly different execution durations per      
          warp. Reducing stalls indicated on the Warp State Statistics and Source Counters sections can help, too.
